newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians protest at wage, pension arrears.
newsitem.headline: Russians protest at wage, pension arrears.

text.p: Workers took to the streets across Russia in strikes and demonstrations on Thursday in a day of protests against unpaid pensions and wages.

But the number of marchers in each city numbered in the tens rather than hundreds of thousands. There were no early reports of violence, although many people called on the government and President Boris Yeltsin to quit.

"This is a political strike. We are going to pass a motion of no confidence in the president," said a defence worker in the industrial and high-technology city of Novosibirsk, three time zones and 3,000 km (1,900 miles) east of Moscow.
Police said up to 20,000 people were marching in the city, which has a population of 1.5 million.
Trade unions and Russia's communist-led opposition, bitter at the fact that millions of workers have not been paid for months, launched their call for protest action weeks ago.
They said they expected 20 million people to take part, but early turnout indicated the numbers would be less than that.

The protests are the first test for a new cabinet appointed over the last month and will give an outlet to frustrations which have built up in the six years of economic reform -- a painful process which has opened a gulf between rich and poor.
Ministers, some appointed in a major government reshuffle this month, admit workers and pensioners are owed 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion), including 10 trillion from the state.
They have promised to resolve the wage crisis as quickly as possible. But new first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov have also pledged to speed up reforms.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told his new cabinet the protests were a "vivid and objective measure" of the seriousness of the problem and he said the government would not ignore them.

The demonstrations started in the Russian Far East and trade unions said 50,000 people had joined a march in the Pacific port city of Vladivostok, a colourful procession of people and red flags which snaked its way through town.
Police put the number at just 15,000.
"I want to live without shocks and without Yeltsin's therapy," read one banner, referring to the economic reforms the president is trying to introduce in Russia.
Yeltsin has said he is concerned at the non-payments and he signed a decree on Thursday aiming at tightening control over budget money allocated to pay the arrears.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin, out of action with heart problems and pneumonia for eight months from last July, was spending the day at the official Gorky-9 residence outside Moscow.
The protests were far from universal.
Union leaders from the miners, long Russia's most militant workers and a group hit hard by pay arrears, said they were not striking and were not calling on Yeltsin's government to quit.
The miners backed Yeltsin in his early struggles against the communists but dislike many of his current policies. They have decided to give the new government a chance, however.
Many factories are already at a standstill and firms in the key metals and energy sectors said output would not be affected. Air traffic controllers do not plan to strike.

In the southern city of Krasnodar, an agricultural centre at the heart of the communist Red Belt, even optimistic trade union leaders expected just 25,000 people of the half-million population to join rallies -- half as many as last May Day.
"There really aren't as big squares in Krasnodar as in Moscow and we have to think of people's safety," said Olympiada Chumakova, deputy head of the local trade union.

In Yeltsin's home Urals region around Yekaterinburg some 25,000 people were expected to demonstrate. Police said 500 protesters had blocked the main Siberian highway in the president's home district of Talitsky.
Yekaterinburg, a closed city in Soviet times, has a large number of defence industry firms, many of which have found it hard to cope with the tough new world of market economics.

The changes, designed to transform the Soviet-era centrally planned economy into a market system modelled on that in the West, have brought colourful goods into Russia's once-bare shops. But millions of people cannot afford to buy.

In Moscow about 500 people protested in the central Tver Street, but they were almost outnumbered by police and OMON police commandos. The main demonstrations in the capital are due to start after 2 p.m. (1100 GMT).
